title: Acute conditions & dental trauma
blurb: Triage of urgent calls, knocked-out teeth (what to replant and how to store them), fractured teeth and the Ellis classes, dry socket and bleeding after extractions.
question: A parent phones in a panic: her 9-year-old has knocked out an upper front tooth at football ten minutes ago, and she is holding it by the root in a tissue. Her younger child, aged 4, knocked out a front tooth last week. What do you tell her to do right now, and would the dentist replant both teeth?

teach.h: Acting quickly and within your role
teach.body: Acute conditions come on suddenly and need prompt care: severe toothache, swelling, bleeding after an extraction, dry socket and injuries to the teeth and jaws. Dental nurses often take the first call. Using the practice's triage protocol, you gather the facts, recognise red flags, give agreed first aid advice and book the patient with the right urgency, involving the dentist. You don't diagnose. If an injury doesn't match the story given, follow safeguarding procedures.

children.label: 999 or A&E
children.sub: Swelling affecting breathing, swallowing or the eye; head injury; heavy bleeding

children.label: See today
children.sub: Knocked-out permanent tooth (at once), facial swelling, dry socket, bleeding

children.label: Next available
children.sub: Lost filling or chipped tooth with no pain

teach.h: First aid for a knocked-out permanent tooth

steps.label: Find the tooth
steps.sub: Hold it by the crown, never the root

steps.label: Rinse only if dirty
steps.sub: A few seconds in milk, saline or cold running water; never scrub

steps.label: Replant at once
steps.sub: Push it gently back into the socket, the right way round

steps.label: Hold it in place
steps.sub: Bite on a clean handkerchief or gauze

steps.label: Come straight in
steps.sub: The dentist checks, splints and reviews

teach.caption: The dentist usually fits a flexible splint for about two weeks, checks tetanus cover and plans follow-up, as root canal treatment is often needed.

teach.h: If it can't be replanted, store it in…

rows.label: Saliva (in the cheek, or spit into a cup for a child)

teach.note: The aim is to keep the ligament cells on the root alive until the tooth is replanted.

teach.body: An avulsed deciduous (baby) tooth is not replanted, because pushing it back can damage the permanent tooth developing just above it. Upper permanent central incisors usually erupt at about 7 to 8 years, so a 4-year-old's knocked-out incisor is a deciduous tooth, while a 9-year-old's is almost certainly permanent. Still bring the younger child in so the dentist can check the area and the remaining teeth.

items.label: Replant at the scene
items.sub: Best chance of the tooth surviving

items.label: Then kept in milk or saline
Reviews
items.sub: Pulp tests and radiographs to watch for problems

teach.caption: Higher classes cover root fractures, displaced teeth and injuries to deciduous teeth. The deeper the fracture, the more urgent: an exposed pulp needs prompt protection.

teach.body: Dry socket happens when the blood clot in an extraction socket breaks down or is lost, leaving bare bone. Typically 2 to 4 days after the extraction the patient has severe throbbing pain, often spreading to the ear, with a bad taste or smell and an empty-looking socket. Risks include smoking, difficult lower molar extractions and rinsing too soon. The dentist irrigates the socket with warm saline, may place a soothing dressing, and advises pain relief. Antibiotics are not usually needed.

teach.h: A fresh socket with its blood clot
teach.caption: Item 6 shows a fresh extraction socket filled with blood clot. In dry socket this clot is lost. Items 1, 3 and 5 show a surgical tray, a kidney dish with gauze and sutures; bleeding is controlled by biting firmly on damp gauze for 15 to 20 minutes.

teach.text: Avulsed PERMANENT tooth: replant immediately, or store in milk or saline and come straight in. Avulsed DECIDUOUS tooth: never replant. And never store a tooth in tap water or wrapped dry in a tissue.

items: Triage with the practice protocol; swelling affecting breathing, swallowing or the eye means 999 or A&E.
Hold an avulsed tooth by the crown; replant at once or store in milk, saline or saliva.
Ellis: I enamel, II dentine, III pulp, IV non-vital, V avulsion.
Dry socket: lost clot, severe pain at 2–4 days; irrigate and dress, no routine antibiotics.

summary: You can now triage urgent calls, give correct first aid for a knocked-out tooth, decide what to replant and how to store a tooth, classify fractures with the Ellis system, and recognise and support the management of dry socket and post-extraction bleeding.

A.q: A parent rings to say their 10-year-old has just knocked out an upper central incisor. Which advice is correct?
options: Wrap it in a dry tissue and come in
Scrub the root clean, then bring it in
Hold it by the crown and replant it now
Leave it out until the dentist sees it
A.why: A 10-year-old's upper central incisor is permanent, so it should be held by the crown and replanted immediately for the best outcome.

whyNot.0: A tooth kept dry loses the living cells on its root.
whyNot.1: Scrubbing destroys the ligament cells needed for the tooth to reattach.
whyNot.3: Delay greatly reduces the chance of the tooth surviving.

A.q: A 4-year-old has knocked out an upper front tooth. What should happen to the tooth?
options: It should not be replanted
It should be replanted at once
It should be stored in milk to replant
It should be splinted for two weeks
A.why: Avulsed deciduous teeth are not replanted, because this can damage the developing permanent tooth.

whyNot.1: Replanting a baby tooth risks harming the permanent successor.
whyNot.2: Storing it is pointless because a deciduous tooth won't be replanted.
whyNot.3: Splinting applies to replanted permanent teeth.

A.q: A patient phones three days after a lower molar extraction with severe throbbing pain spreading to the ear and a bad taste. What is the most likely cause?
options: Normal healing pain
Dry socket
A periodontal abscess
Local anaesthetic wearing off
A.why: Severe pain 2 to 4 days after an extraction, radiating to the ear with a bad taste, is typical of dry socket (alveolar osteitis).

whyNot.0: Normal healing pain eases day by day rather than getting severe at day three.
whyNot.2: A periodontal abscess is linked to a periodontal pocket, not a recent socket.
whyNot.3: Local anaesthetic wears off within hours, not days.

B.q: An avulsed permanent tooth can't be replanted at the scene. Which is the best storage medium?
options: Tap water
A dry tissue
Cold milk
Mouthwash
B.why: Milk keeps the root's ligament cells alive until the tooth can be replanted; saline or saliva are alternatives.

whyNot.0: Tap water damages the root cells because it is not balanced to body fluids.
whyNot.1: A dry tooth quickly loses its living root cells.
whyNot.3: Mouthwash contains chemicals that harm the root cells.

B.q: A tooth has fractured through enamel and dentine, but the pulp is not exposed. Which Ellis class is this?
options: Class I
Class II
Class III
Class IV
B.why: Ellis Class II is a fracture involving enamel and dentine without pulp exposure.

whyNot.2: Class III involves exposure of the pulp.
whyNot.3: Class IV describes a non-vital tooth.

B.q: A caller says his face has swollen so much since this morning that his eye is closing and he is finding it hard to swallow. What should you advise?
options: Take painkillers and call again tomorrow
Book the next routine check-up
Rinse with warm salt water tonight
Go to A&E or call 999 now
B.why: Swelling affecting the eye or swallowing can threaten the airway and needs emergency hospital care.

whyNot.0: Waiting could allow the swelling to block the airway.
whyNot.1: This is an emergency, not a routine problem.
whyNot.2: Salt water rinses won't treat a spreading infection.

C.q: How should a knocked-out permanent tooth be picked up?
options: By the root, to protect the crown
By the crown, avoiding the root
With tissue wrapped round the root
By either end, as long as gloves are on
C.why: Holding the crown protects the delicate ligament cells on the root, which the tooth needs to reattach.

whyNot.0: Touching the root damages the cells needed for healing.
whyNot.2: Tissue rubs and dries the root surface.
whyNot.3: Gloves don't stop the root cells being damaged by handling.

C.q: Which management is typical for dry socket?
options: Extract the tooth next to the socket
Prescribe antibiotics and send the patient home
Advise vigorous rinsing every hour
Irrigate with warm saline and dress the socket
C.why: The socket is gently irrigated with warm saline and a soothing dressing may be placed; pain relief is advised.

whyNot.0: Neighbouring teeth aren't the cause of dry socket.
whyNot.1: Dry socket isn't an infection that routinely needs antibiotics.
whyNot.2: Vigorous rinsing can disturb healing further.

C.q: A child's injury doesn't match the explanation given by the adult with them, and you notice other bruises. What should you do?
options: Ignore it as it's not a dental matter
Ask the child to explain alone at length
Follow the practice safeguarding procedure
Phone the child's school for their view
C.why: An injury that doesn't fit the story is a safeguarding concern, so you follow the practice procedure and involve the safeguarding lead.

whyNot.0: The dental team has a duty to act on safeguarding concerns.
whyNot.1: Questioning a child at length isn't your role and may harm an investigation.
whyNot.3: Contacting the school yourself breaches confidentiality and bypasses the procedure.

reteach.title: Treat a knocked-out tooth like a plant pulled from the soil
reteach.question: If a plant is pulled up, what would you do to give it the best chance? How does that match a knocked-out tooth?

blocks.body: A pulled-up plant survives if you put it straight back in the soil and don't let its roots dry out or get scraped. A tooth is the same: the 'roots' that matter are the living ligament cells on the root surface. So hold it by the crown, put it straight back, and if you can't, keep it in milk or saline. Tap water and dry tissue kill those cells. But a baby tooth is like a plant with a seedling growing underneath: pushing it back could crush the new one.

children.label: Replant now
children.sub: Or milk or saline, and come straight in

blocks.text: If you're unsure whether the tooth is deciduous or permanent, treat it as permanent and get the patient seen straight away. The dentist will decide.

explain.body: Use the practice protocol. Swelling affecting breathing, swallowing or the eye, heavy bleeding or a head injury means 999 or A&E. Avulsed permanent teeth, facial swelling, dry socket and bleeding are seen urgently.

test.q: Which caller should be advised to go to A&E or call 999?
options: A lost filling with no pain
A chipped tooth that feels sharp
Swelling affecting their swallowing
A loose crown that came off at lunch
test.why: Swelling that affects swallowing can threaten the airway, so it is a medical emergency.

whyNot.0: A painless lost filling is routine.
whyNot.1: A sharp chipped tooth can be seen routinely or soon.
whyNot.3: A loose crown is not an emergency.

explain.body: Permanent tooth: hold by the crown, rinse briefly only if dirty, replant at once, bite on gauze and come straight in. If it can't go back, store in milk, saline or saliva. Deciduous tooth: never replant.

test.q: Why must an avulsed tooth never be stored in tap water?
options: It damages the living cells on the root
It makes the tooth too slippery to hold
It stains the crown of the tooth
It dissolves the enamel quickly
test.why: Tap water isn't balanced to body fluids, so it swells and kills the ligament cells on the root.

whyNot.1: Slipperiness isn't the concern; root cell survival is.

explain.body: I: enamel only. II: enamel and dentine. III: pulp exposed. IV: tooth non-vital. V: tooth lost. Deeper injuries are more urgent.

test.q: A fractured incisor has a pink spot showing in the middle of the broken surface. Which Ellis class does this suggest?
options: Class I
Class II
Class III
Class V
test.why: A pink or bleeding spot means the pulp is exposed, which is Ellis Class III.

whyNot.0: Class I is an enamel-only chip.
whyNot.1: Class II reaches dentine but the pulp isn't exposed.
whyNot.3: Class V is a tooth that has been knocked out.

explain.body: Dry socket: clot lost, severe throbbing pain at 2 to 4 days, bad taste. Irrigate, dress, pain relief. Bleeding after extraction: bite firmly on damp gauze for 15 to 20 minutes; if it won't stop, come back in.

test.q: Which factor increases the risk of dry socket?
options: Smoking soon after the extraction
Resting quietly for the evening
Eating soft food on the other side
Taking paracetamol as directed
test.why: Smoking reduces blood supply and can dislodge the clot, increasing the risk of dry socket.

whyNot.2: Chewing on the other side protects the socket.
whyNot.3: Paracetamol for pain doesn't increase dry socket risk.
